Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. The curator spent months deciding which paintings to display in the museum's collections. — CURATOR (n) = người phụ trách trưng bày, giám tuyển; collocation "a museum curator"; đừng nhầm với "creator".

2. Some critics accuse opera houses of elitism, arguing that they only cater to a small, privileged group. — ELITISM (n) = chủ nghĩa tinh hoa; collocation cố định "accuse sb of elitism"; danh từ không đếm được.

3. The ancient sculpture was considered priceless because no one could put a monetary value on it. — PRICELESS (adj) = vô giá (quá quý để định giá); collocation "a priceless masterpiece/artefact"; trái nghĩa gần như "worthless" dù cấu tạo từ giống nhau.

4. A wealthy patron provided the funding that allowed the young sculptor to complete her first major exhibition. — PATRON (n) = nhà bảo trợ; collocation "a wealthy patron", "patron of the arts"; đừng nhầm với "patient".
5. The national gallery serves as a repository for the country's most important paintings. — REPOSITORY (n) = kho lưu trữ; đi với giới từ "for/of", không phải "in"; số nhiều "repositories".

6. Many people believe the government should subsidise theatres so that ticket prices stay affordable. — SUBSIDISE (v) = trợ cấp, hỗ trợ tài chính từ ngân sách công; chính tả Anh-Anh "-ise"; danh từ tương ứng "subsidy".

7. For centuries, royal patronage allowed composers and painters to devote themselves entirely to their craft. — PATRONAGE (n) = sự bảo trợ (tài chính); collocation "royal patronage", "state patronage of the arts"; đừng nhầm với "patronising" (kẻ cả).

8. The gallery's new exhibition featured avant-garde installations that unsettled many traditional visitors. — AVANT-GARDE (adj) = tiên phong, thử nghiệm; giữ nguyên gạch nối vì là từ mượn tiếng Pháp; collocation "avant-garde art/theatre".

9. The novel's descriptions of the war were so evocative that they brought vivid, disturbing images to readers' minds. — EVOCATIVE (adj) = gợi cảm xúc/hình ảnh mạnh; đừng nhầm với "provocative" (khiêu khích).

10. Knowing about classical music and fine art can quietly help a person accumulate cultural capital in certain social circles. — CULTURAL CAPITAL (n phrase) = vốn văn hoá; thuật ngữ xã hội học, không đếm được, không có số nhiều.

11. Only a true connoisseur of fine wine and painting would spot such a subtle technique. — CONNOISSEUR (n) = người sành sỏi, am hiểu tinh tường; collocation "a true connoisseur"; phát âm cuối /-sɜː/ không phải /z/.

12. Free entry to national museums is one way of democratising access to culture for people from all income levels. — DEMOCRATISING ACCESS (n phrase) = dân chủ hoá khả năng tiếp cận; collocation "democratising access to sth"; chính tả Anh-Anh "-ise".
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu
1. Band 7: Free admission to museums would give people from all walks of life the chance to appreciate art.
Band 8: Were national museums to abolish admission fees, art would arguably become far more democratised, though such a policy is only sustainable when paired with robust public funding.
2. Band 7: Governments should subsidise artists financially so that they can continue producing meaningful work.
Band 8: Sustained government subsidy, rather than sporadic grants, is arguably what allows artists to pursue ambitious, long-term projects without being driven purely by commercial pressures.
3. Band 7: Many people find contemporary art challenging to interpret, as it often abandons familiar conventions.
Band 8: The perceived inaccessibility of much avant-garde art stems less from its subject matter than from its deliberate departure from the conventions audiences have come to expect.
4. Band 7: Music is often regarded as a universal language capable of conveying emotions that words fail to capture.
Band 8: Music's capacity to evoke emotion without relying on language is precisely what lends credence to the notion that it functions as a universal language transcending cultural boundaries.
5. Band 7: Wealthy collectors are often willing to pay extraordinary sums for paintings regarded as priceless masterpieces.
Band 8: The extraordinary sums that high-net-worth patrons pay for ostensibly priceless masterpieces say as much about status and cultural capital as they do about aesthetic merit.
6. Band 7: Traditional art forms are gradually being overshadowed by digital and online forms of creative expression.
Band 8: As digital and algorithmically-generated art gain traction, traditional forms are being not so much replaced as recontextualised within an increasingly hybrid creative landscape.
7. Band 7: Schools should incorporate more art and music lessons into the curriculum to nurture children's creativity.
Band 8: Embedding art and music more firmly within the curriculum would arguably foster creativity in ways that purely academic subjects are ill-equipped to achieve.
8. Band 7: Watching a live theatre performance tends to have a far greater emotional impact than viewing a recorded version.
Band 8: The immediacy and unpredictability inherent in live theatre generate a visceral impact that even the most polished recorded reproduction can rarely replicate.

passages.text: For nearly two decades, advocates of arts education have drawn on a growing neuroscientific literature to argue that musical training reshapes the developing brain in ways that benefit cognition more broadly. Brightly coloured brain images, often produced by magnetic resonance scanners and reproduced in policy briefs, appear to show thicker grey matter in regions associated with hearing, motor control and even mathematical reasoning. The implication, frequently drawn by ministers and school principals, is that lessons in violin or piano may improve a child's academic performance well beyond the music room itself. This narrative has been powerful enough to influence funding decisions in several countries, yet a careful look at the underlying evidence suggests that it has been substantially oversold.
passages.title: The Promise and the Problem

passages.text: One of the most prolific researchers in the field is Professor Gottfried Schlaug, formerly of Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston. Schlaug's group has produced a long series of papers, beginning in the late 1990s, documenting structural and functional differences between the brains of trained musicians and those of non-musicians. Some of these differences appear early in training and become more pronounced over years of practice. Schlaug himself has been cautious in interpreting them, generally arguing only that musical training is associated with measurable neural change, and that further study is required before claims of transfer to unrelated academic domains can be confidently made. His careful framing, the author observes, has not always been respected by those who quote his findings in popular outlets.
passages.title: The Promise and the Problem

passages.text: A blunter critique has come from Dr Giovanni Sala of the University of Liverpool, whose meta-analyses of intervention studies have generated considerable attention since 2017. Sala and his colleagues examined more than fifty randomised or quasi-randomised trials in which children were assigned to music lessons or to a comparison activity, and the effects of training were measured on tests of general cognitive ability and academic achievement. After correcting for publication bias — the well-documented tendency for positive findings to reach print while null results languish in filing cabinets — Sala reported that the average effect of music training on far-transfer outcomes was close to zero. Near-transfer to specifically musical skills was, unsurprisingly, robust; but the wider claim that music makes children smarter, in any general sense, was not, in his reading, supported.
passages.title: The Promise and the Problem

passages.text: Sala's conclusions have been resisted by researchers who argue that meta-analyses cannot capture the long-term, social and developmental benefits that interventions of this kind may confer. Professor Assal Habibi of the University of Southern California has led a longitudinal study of children from low-income backgrounds enrolled in intensive, orchestra-based programmes modelled on Venezuela's El Sistema. Over five years, Habibi's team documented changes in auditory processing, executive function and prosocial behaviour that, she contends, are unlikely to emerge from the brief and often diluted interventions that dominate the meta-analytic record. The author, although broadly sympathetic to Sala's methodological discipline, regards Habibi's argument as serious, particularly where the comparison condition in short trials is itself a structured group activity rather than no activity at all.
passages.title: The Promise and the Problem

passages.text: A more balanced summary has come from Professor Ellen Winner of Boston College, whose 2018 book on the cognitive benefits of arts education attempted to separate well-evidenced claims from weakly supported ones. Winner concludes, broadly in line with Sala, that confident assertions of academic transfer rest on shaky ground. Yet she also argues, in agreement with parts of Habibi's view, that musical training reliably develops specifically musical skills, and that arts education can be defended on its own terms — as a humane and culturally rich form of learning — without being dressed up as a tool for raising mathematics scores. The author finds Winner's separation of these two arguments particularly helpful, and shares her suspicion that the academic-transfer rhetoric has, on balance, harmed rather than helped the cause of music in schools.
passages.title: The Promise and the Problem

passages.text: Several mechanisms appear to be at work when popular accounts simplify this literature. Researchers under pressure to attract funding may, perhaps understandably, emphasise the more striking implications of their findings. Journalists, working to tight deadlines, may compress a hedged claim into a confident headline. Brain images, with their suggestive splashes of colour, lend an air of biological authority to claims about behaviour that the imaging data themselves cannot, on close inspection, support. Policymakers, particularly those without specialist scientific training, may take a single striking finding as definitive when the underlying field is far less settled than the headline suggests, and may then build budget decisions on a foundation that careful reading would have refused to provide. The author suspects that none of these participants acts in bad faith; the cumulative effect, however, is a public discourse in which careful researchers find their work used to justify policies they would themselves regard as poorly grounded.
passages.title: The Promise and the Problem

passages.text: None of this should be read as an argument against music in schools. The author maintains that there are substantial reasons to support such programmes, including the long-standing benefits of group performance for cooperation and persistence, the intrinsic value of musical literacy, and the demonstrable improvements in specifically musical and possibly auditory skills that careful training produces. What the evidence does not yet support is the inflated claim that two terms of recorder lessons will raise standardised test scores across the curriculum. Defending arts education on honest grounds — that is, on its inherent worth and on the narrower benefits that the evidence currently does support — seems both more defensible and, in the long run, considerably more sustainable than continuing to overstate what neuroscience has actually shown.

audio_scripts.text: Right, settle in. Today's tutorial — we're, um, hearing from Hiroko and Tomas on music-and-brain research methodology. Hiroko, you wanna kick us off? And for the recording, could you spell your surname for me?

Yeah, sure. So I'm Hiroko Tanizaki — that's T-A-N-I-Z-A-K-I, the Z is a soft Z, not a hard German Z. My project was a longitudinal study tracking forty-four adult string-instrument learners across the Eastgate Conservatoire region. (Q1)

Erm, the pilot ran in 2021 — sorry, no, 2020 — and the main wave concluded in 2024. So four years end to end. Originally we'd planned to wrap up in 2023, but lab access restrictions, you know, pushed everything back by twelve months. (Q2)
Okay. Tense-wise, just to clarify for the recording — your fMRI data collection FINISHED in 2024, you're publishing this year, correct?
Right. Published 2026, but the next cohort we're gonna scan starts in 2028.

Well, the dominant theoretical lens here is what Élodie Trémaine called the "auditory-motor coupling framework". And just to flag the terminology — you'll see related labels in the older neuroscience literature: rhythmic entrainment, sensorimotor synchronisation, beat-induced motor activation. All those describe the same construct, more or less. The current scholarly term, though, is auditory-motor coupling. I'll stick with that. (Q3)

Yeah, and I'm gonna echo Hiroko's framing. In my sample — twenty-five adult amateur singers across two community choirs — most of the singers exhibited measurable left-hemisphere lateralisation gains after twelve weeks of structured ear-training. Actually, sorry, let me be precise — nineteen out of twenty-five, so roughly seventy-six per cent. Only a few — about twelve per cent — showed no measurable shift, and some — twelve per cent — showed right-hemisphere gains instead. (Q4)
Right. Now, Hiroko, did your sample confirm the "musical training necessarily expands grey-matter volume" thesis?

Sorta, yeah, but with caveats. Most of the learners I scanned did NOT exhibit the grey-matter volumetric expansion that the early literature predicted. The implicit dose-response contract, well, has shifted. Today's neuroscientists see white-matter integrity, particularly in the arcuate fasciculus, as more diagnostic than raw cortical volume. Only a small minority — fewer than fourteen per cent — displayed the classical volumetric expansion. (Q5)

And, dunno about you, but I found something interesting on the listening-genre-diversity axis. So-called genre-cross-training — where amateur musicians deliberately rotate through classical, jazz, and folk listening — that's actually expanding sharply in conservatoire curricula. And the literature suggests this constrains a learner's tendency toward stylistic over-specialisation.
Hmm. Hiroko, did you control for prior-training stratum?
Kinda. We stratified by years of childhood training. Counter-intuitively, the LATE-STARTER quartile — adults who began after thirty — showed the steepest plasticity gains, not the long-trained group.
Well, it's about ceiling effects — long-trained players have less headroom for visible change.

And one final thing — practice-spacing data. In learners who practised in three short daily blocks, retention was, um, considerably higher than in learners who practised in one long weekly session. Researchers attribute it to consolidation cycles during sleep.

Right. Now, going back to what Hiroko mentioned at the start — that "current scholarly term" — that's the construct we'll operationalise next week. Oh, and Tomas, on your seventy-six-per-cent figure: the implication that ear-training drives lateralisation aligns with Trémaine, but Hiroko's volumetric finding qualifies it. Good tension. Thanks both. (Q6)

Phía trợ cấp công (subsidy-first):
•  Nghệ thuật là hàng hoá công và kho di sản dân tộc; vé miễn phí/giá rẻ giúp mọi tầng lớp tiếp cận.
•  Thiếu tiền công, giá vé tăng và nhiều bảo tàng vùng phải đóng cửa, biến nghệ thuật thành đặc quyền của giới giàu.
•  Trợ cấp ổn định bảo vệ các thiết chế khỏi biến động thị trường và sở thích nhất thời của nhà tài trợ.
Phía tài trợ tư nhân (patronage-first):
•  Nhà tài trợ và doanh nghiệp linh hoạt, rót vốn nhanh cho dự án tham vọng mà bộ máy nhà nước khó theo kịp.
•  Tín hiệu thị trường giúp lọc bỏ tác phẩm không tìm được khán giả; hiệu ứng Bilbao cho thấy đầu tư tư nhân hồi sinh đô thị.
•  Phụ thuộc hoàn toàn vào tiền thuế khiến nghệ thuật lệ thuộc vào ưu tiên chính trị thay đổi liên tục.
•  Introduction — paraphrase: two maps of the Northgate gallery, 2010 and 2024, after a major redevelopment.
•  Overview — net impact: the site was expanded, modernised and made more visitor-friendly; parking moved underground (no specific features).
•  Body 1 — describe the 2010 layout in the past simple: compact footprint, courtyard, gravel car park.
•  Body 2 — describe the 2024 changes using past/present perfect passive: additions, replacements and the enclosed atrium.

band_comparison.text: Band 8 mở đoạn Overview bằng những cụm từ tổng hợp giàu hình ảnh ("the dominant impression is one of expansion", "surface parking has given way to landscaped public space") thay vì liệt kê rời rạc từng thay đổi như Band 7, giúp câu tổng quan cô đọng và có tầm nhìn bao quát hơn. Về ngữ pháp, Band 8 đan xen quá khứ hoàn thành bị động với liên từ chỉ phương hướng trong cùng một câu (ví dụ cấu trúc kiểu "to the east... had been absorbed", "to the west... had been enclosed"), thể hiện Grammatical Range chặt chẽ và đa dạng hơn hẳn. Về từ vựng, Band 8 sử dụng lớp từ chính xác và biến hoá cao ("built fabric", "repurposed", "absorbed into", "rerouted", "given way to") cùng các trạng từ đánh giá tinh tế, trong khi Band 7 có xu hướng lặp lại các động từ đơn giản như "replaced" và "converted" nhiều lần hơn, khiến bài viết kém đa dạng hơn về mặt diễn đạt.

blocks.text: The two maps depict the Northgate Contemporary Art Gallery as it existed in 2010 and as it appears in 2024, following a substantial redevelopment that has reshaped both interior and exterior spaces.

Overall, the site has undergone considerable expansion and modernisation: visitor-facing facilities have been enlarged, parking moved underground, and the open courtyard fully enclosed. These changes appear designed to boost footfall and broaden the gallery's appeal.

In 2010, the gallery occupied a compact rectangular footprint, with the Permanent Collection in the north wing and the Temporary Exhibition Hall opposite. A modest café and ticket desk lay on the eastern side, while the western courtyard housed outdoor sculpture; a gravel car park with twenty spaces sat to the rear, served by a single eastern entrance.

By 2024, the Permanent Collection had been doubled in area and supplemented by a Digital Art Suite, while the south wing gained an Education and Workshop Centre. The café has been replaced by a glass-fronted Visitor Hub, the courtyard enclosed within a covered atrium, and the rear car park converted into a landscaped sculpture garden, with parking relocated underground. A second entrance has also been added from the south.
The two maps depict the Northgate Contemporary Art Gallery in 2010 and in 2024, following an ambitious redevelopment that has transformed both its built fabric and its grounds.

Overall, the dominant impression is one of expansion and modernisation: every wing has been enlarged or repurposed, the once-open courtyard has been enclosed, and surface parking has given way to landscaped public space, apparently to widen access and broaden appeal.

In 2010, the gallery occupied a single-storey footprint. The Permanent Collection sat in the north wing, opposite the Temporary Exhibition Hall, while a small café and ticket desk lined the eastern edge. To the west lay an open courtyard with sculpture, while a gravel car park of twenty spaces, reached from a single eastern entrance, occupied the rear.

By 2024, the transformation was comprehensive. The Permanent Collection had been doubled and supplemented by a Digital Art Suite, while the south wing acquired an Education and Workshop Centre. The eastern café was absorbed into a Visitor Hub with accessible ticketing, and the western courtyard enclosed within an atrium. The car park had been replaced by a landscaped sculpture garden, with vehicles rerouted to an eighty-space underground facility reached by a new southern entrance.

Band 8 cũng dẫn chứng sắc bén và cụ thể hơn ("re-engineered their tax codes", "constrained by electoral cycles") kết hợp với mật độ danh hoá cao ("the dichotomy is false", "exclusive reliance on subsidy"), qua đó nâng điểm Task Response và Lexical Resource. Về cohesion, Band 8 dùng dấu gạch ngang xen giữa để nhấn mạnh ("complemented — not replaced — by") và các liên từ học thuật tinh tế ("Equally serious, however", "in my considered view"), tạo văn phong nhất quán và trang trọng hơn hẳn so với bản Band 7.

blocks.text: Exposure to evocative works of art from an early age cultivates an aesthetic sensibility that enriches a person's emotional life well beyond the classroom.
Contemporary art frequently challenges the status quo, provoking the kind of critical thinking that more conventional subjects rarely demand.
A thriving arts scene accumulates valuable cultural capital for a city, drawing visitors and prestige in ways that pure economic output cannot.
For a talented busker or emerging musician, public performance offers a rare, low-cost route to building an audience without institutional patronage.
Without state subsidised access, the arts risk becoming a domain of elitism, where only the wealthy can appreciate genuine masterpieces.
Museums that depend heavily on wealthy patrons may feel pressure to curate exhibitions that flatter their benefactors rather than serve artistic merit.
The rise of digital reproduction has arguably diluted the aesthetic impact of viewing an original masterpiece in person.
Avant-garde installations, however intellectually ambitious, can alienate general audiences who find them inaccessible or self-indulgent.
Declining public funding for arts education has forced many schools to abandon programmes that once nurtured a broad appreciation of aesthetics.
The emergence of non-fungible token art reflects a deeper cultural shift in how ownership and authenticity are now understood in a digital age.
A long tradition of state patronage, dating back centuries, explains why certain nations continue to produce a disproportionate share of celebrated composers and painters.
Urban regeneration strategies increasingly rely on iconic, avant-garde museum architecture to attract cultural tourism and revive struggling local economies.
Free admission to major galleries has been shown to democratise access to culture, drawing visitors who would otherwise never encounter a genuine masterpiece.
A decline in state subsidised theatre has pushed ticket prices beyond the reach of many working-class families.
The proliferation of installation art has broadened public expectations of what a museum experience can offer beyond static exhibitions.
Sustained government patronage of the arts can, over time, transform a modest regional gallery into a globally recognised repository of cultural heritage.
Curators face the persistent challenge of balancing crowd-pleasing exhibitions against the responsibility to preserve priceless artefacts from overexposure.
Reconciling free public access with the immense cost of climate control and conservation for priceless collections remains an unresolved dilemma for most institutions.
Convincing sceptical high-net-worth patrons to fund avant-garde work, rather than safely conventional pieces, is a constant struggle for emerging artists.
Arts institutions must continually justify public subsidised funding against competing demands from healthcare and education budgets.

idea_sections.heading: 5. Problems / Challenges — Vấn đề / Thách thức

blocks.text: Offering free entry on designated days can democratise access without abandoning the subsidised revenue that admission fees on other days provide.
Partnering contemporary artists with schools can help rebuild the arts appreciation that budget cuts have eroded.
Diversifying funding sources, rather than relying solely on a handful of high-net-worth patrons, would make galleries more resilient to economic downturns.
Digitising priceless collections allows global audiences to engage with a nation's artistic heritage without physically endangering fragile originals.
Many people firmly believe that governments have a moral obligation to subsidise the arts as a vital component of national heritage.
Others contend that if an art form is genuinely valuable, it ought to survive through commercial demand rather than public patronage.
There is widespread agreement that music functions as something close to a universal language, transcending barriers that spoken language cannot.
Some argue that avant-garde art is often praised out of intellectual conformity rather than genuine aesthetic merit.

idea_sections.heading: 7. Popular opinions — Quan điểm phổ biến

blocks.text: National governments bear significant responsibility for ensuring that subsidised access to museums does not become a privilege reserved for the elite.
Curators have a duty to make evocative works accessible through clear interpretation, rather than assuming visitors already possess deep cultural capital.
Wealthy patrons and corporations arguably owe a debt to the communities that host them, which philanthropic patronage of local galleries could help repay.
Educators are responsible for introducing children to contemporary as well as classical art, broadening appreciation beyond a narrow canon.

idea_sections.heading: 8. Who is responsible — Trách nhiệm thuộc về ai

blocks.text: While critics decry elitism in the art world, defenders note that free public museums have done more than almost any other institution to democratise culture.
Although avant-garde work is often dismissed as inaccessible, some of today's most celebrated masterpieces were once considered radical departures from convention.
It is sometimes argued that private patronage compromises artistic independence, yet history shows that state funding can carry equally restrictive political strings.
Sceptics who view non-fungible token art as a passing fad overlook the genuine questions it raises about authorship and ownership in the digital era.
As digital platforms gain significant traction, physical exhibitions may increasingly be complemented by immersive virtual galleries accessible to a global audience.
Growing interest in non-fungible token art suggests that definitions of an original masterpiece will continue to evolve alongside technology.
Museums are likely to rely ever more on interactive installation art to compete for the attention of digitally native younger visitors.
Public pressure may eventually force wealthier institutions to share high-net-worth patron funding with smaller, under-resourced regional galleries.

idea_sections.heading: 10. Future trends / predictions — Xu hướng tương lai

blocks.text: Whereas contemporary art often prioritises conceptual provocation, traditional art is more commonly admired for its technical craftsmanship and evocative realism.
Compared with earlier centuries, when patronage depended almost entirely on aristocrats, today's arts funding draws on a far broader mix of state and private sources.
Unlike a static exhibition of historic artefacts, an interactive installation invites visitors to participate directly in the artistic experience.
In contrast to elitist perceptions of opera and ballet, street performance by a talented busker remains one of the most genuinely accessible art forms.
The so-called "Bilbao effect," in which an iconic avant-garde museum revitalised a struggling industrial city, is frequently cited as evidence of the arts' economic potential.
A well-known case of a priceless masterpiece being restored after decades of neglect illustrates the vital role that subsidised conservation programmes play.
Museum visitor statistics comparing free-entry and paid-entry periods provide measurable evidence of how pricing affects the democratiseation of access.
A personal anecdote about discovering an evocative piece of contemporary art that reshaped one's worldview can effectively anchor an argument in a Speaking or Writing response.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: The question of how the arts should be funded — through generous government subsidy or through private patronage — has long divided cultural policymakers. Although both models have something to offer, I believe public funding must remain the backbone of arts policy.

Supporters of heavy subsidy point out that the arts are repositories of national heritage and therefore a public good. What organisations such as the Arts Council in the United Kingdom tend to emphasise is accessibility: free or low-cost entry to museums, galleries and theatres ensures that cultural appreciation is not confined to the wealthy. Without public money, ticket prices would likely rise, and many regional institutions would face existential financial pressure, leaving the arts as a domain of elitism rather than shared inheritance.

Those who prefer private patronage, by contrast, argue that philanthropy research shows donors to be more flexible and responsive than ministries. Wealthy patrons and corporate sponsors can finance ambitious projects quickly, and market signals can help filter out work that fails to find an audience. Iconic cultural buildings, such as the Guggenheim Bilbao's mixed-funding model, have been built largely through private giving and have revitalised entire urban economies.

In my view, relying exclusively on either model would be unwise. Subsidy alone risks creating dependence on shifting political priorities, while private patronage alone tends to concentrate cultural power among a small donor class. A hybrid system, with state funding as the floor and philanthropy as a supplement, seems the most balanced approach.

To conclude, while both public subsidy and private patronage have legitimate roles, I lean toward continued government support as the central pillar. This is the only arrangement that genuinely safeguards both artistic accessibility and the cultural heritage that defines a nation.

Few questions in cultural policy are as contested as how the arts ought to be funded. While advocates of heavy state subsidy and proponents of private patronage each marshal substantial arguments, my position is that public funding must remain the structural backbone, complemented — not replaced — by philanthropy.

Those who defend generous subsidy argue, with considerable force, that the arts function as repositories of collective heritage and therefore meet the classical definition of a public good. What Arts Council research consistently demonstrates is that subsidised entry democratises access: were museums and regional theatres reliant solely on ticket revenue, they would almost certainly drift toward elitism, catering predominantly to affluent urban audiences. Public investment, in this view, is what prevents the arts from becoming the exclusive preserve of the well-off.

Equally serious, however, is the case for private patronage. Philanthropy research suggests that donors and corporate sponsors tend to provide flexible, fast-moving capital that ministries, constrained by electoral cycles, often cannot match. Landmark institutions — the Guggenheim Bilbao among them — illustrate how private giving, intelligently leveraged, can revitalise entire urban economies. So influential has private patronage become in the contemporary art market that several countries have re-engineered their tax codes to encourage cultural donations.

My own view is that the dichotomy is false. Exclusive reliance on subsidy risks subordinating culture to shifting political priorities; exclusive reliance on philanthropy risks concentrating curatorial power in a narrow donor class. A hybrid model — substantial public funding as the floor, philanthropic giving as accelerator — best preserves both accessibility and innovation.

To conclude, although heavy subsidy and private patronage each carry weight, I incline toward a mixed system anchored by public funding. Only such a settlement, in my considered view, can simultaneously safeguard cultural heritage, democratise access, and remain responsive to artistic experimentation.

A. SENTENCE UPGRADE LADDER (5 examples · Band 6 → 7 → 8)
Example 1 — Topic sentence
Band 6: I want to talk about a Picasso painting called Guernica that changed how I see art.
Band 7: The piece that fundamentally reshaped my understanding of what art can do is Picasso's Guernica.
Band 8: What ultimately recalibrated my conception of art's political weight was an unhurried hour spent before Picasso's Guernica at the Reina Sofía. (cleft + nominalisation)

solutions.text: PHẦN A — Viết lại câu (12 items)
Viết lại mỗi câu dưới đây dùng TỪ GỢI Ý (in hoa), giữ nguyên nghĩa và đúng dạng/collocation.
1. The person in charge of organising the museum's collections spent months deciding which paintings to display. (CURATOR)
2. Some critics say opera houses only cater to a small, privileged group of wealthy people. (ELITISM)
3. No one could put a monetary value on the ancient sculpture because it was considered so precious. (PRICELESS)
4. A wealthy businessman provided the funding that allowed the young sculptor to complete her first major exhibition. (PATRON)
5. The national gallery serves as a place where the country's most important paintings are kept and preserved. (REPOSITORY)
6. Many people believe the government should provide financial support to theatres so that ticket prices stay affordable. (SUBSIDISE)
7. For centuries, royal financial support allowed composers and painters to devote themselves entirely to their craft. (PATRONAGE)
8. The gallery's new exhibition featured experimental, boundary-pushing installations that unsettled many traditional visitors. (AVANT-GARDE)
9. The novel's descriptions of the war were so powerful that they brought vivid, disturbing images to readers' minds. (EVOCATIVE)
10. Knowing about classical music and fine art can quietly boost a person's social standing in certain circles. (CULTURAL CAPITAL)
11. Only someone with genuinely expert knowledge of fine wine and painting would spot such a subtle technique. (CONNOISSEUR)

The Decline of Arts Education: Many public schools worldwide are severely cutting budgets for music and arts programmes to focus exclusively on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics) subjects.

2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Funding the Arts (Should the government pay?)

Arguments FOR Funding: The arts are the repositories of a nation's cultural heritage; relying solely on private patrons or ticket sales leads to elitism; subsidising museums democratises culture, making it accessible to low-income families and children.

Arguments AGAINST Funding: Taxpayers' money should be prioritised for essential public services like healthcare, infrastructure, and education; if an art form is truly valuable, it should survive independently through commercial success and public demand.
Topic: Free Museums vs. Admission Fees

For Free Entry: Maximises accessibility and promotes art appreciation across all social classes; encourages frequent, short visits rather than exhausting full-day tours; acts as a valuable supplementary educational resource for schools.

For Admission Fees: High-quality curation, climate control for priceless artefacts, and building maintenance require massive budgets; charging tourists generates significant revenue; free entry often leads to overcrowding, ruining the aesthetic experience.

Contemporary/Abstract Art (Pros): Challenges the status quo and provokes critical thinking; focuses on evoking deep emotions and exploring complex societal issues rather than mere visual replication.

Model answer (≈ 277 words)

The artwork that, more than any other, recalibrated my conception of what art can do is Picasso's Guernica — a piece I encountered, almost by accident, at the Reina Sofía in Madrid in the summer of 2022. I'd seen it reproduced in textbooks since school, but standing in front of the actual canvas was an entirely different proposition.

Stretching nearly eight metres across in a stark monochrome palette, Guernica distils the horror of the 1937 Luftwaffe raid on the Basque town of Guernica into a vocabulary of fragmented limbs, screaming horses, and a single bare lightbulb burning above the carnage. Painted in just over a month, the work was commissioned for the Spanish Pavilion at the Paris International Exposition and has since travelled the world as, arguably, the twentieth century's most enduring anti-war statement.

What I hadn't anticipated was the visceral weight of the encounter. Never had I appreciated quite how forcefully a static image could function as moral testimony. Documentary footage of war, oddly, had never moved me in this way. The painting's monochrome — a deliberate evocation of newsprint — collapses the distance between viewer and atrocity in a way colour somehow cannot.

This is, incidentally, consistent with the emerging neuroaesthetics literature; Chatterjee's foundational 2014 work suggests that visual art activates limbic responses that linguistic accounts often bypass entirely. For me, that hour in the gallery quietly demolished the idea that art is decorative or supplementary. It is, at its strongest, a form of civic memory — a vessel for collective trauma that survives long after the witnesses themselves are gone.
Were I to put it simply: Guernica taught me that art, properly understood, is never neutral.

Q1. Should AI-generated work be considered "real art"?
PEEL answer
Point: I'd take a fairly heterodox view here — AI-generated images can be art, but the locus of authorship is genuinely unsettled.

Evidence: The 2023 US Copyright Office ruling on Zarya of the Dawn explicitly denied protection to purely AI-generated imagery, while a 2024 Nature study by Epstein et al. found that human prompt-engineering substantially shapes aesthetic outcomes, complicating a binary "human vs. machine" framing.

Explanation: What this signals is that traditional notions of authorship — rooted in nineteenth-century romantic individualism — are simply ill-suited to a tool that operates as a generative collaborator rather than a passive brush.
Link: So rather than asking whether AI art is real, the more productive question is what authorship now means in a co-creative pipeline.

I'd take a fairly heterodox view. The 2023 US Copyright Office ruling on Zarya of the Dawn explicitly denied protection to purely AI-generated images, but Epstein and colleagues, writing in Nature in 2024, found that human prompt-engineering substantially shapes aesthetic outcomes. What this signals is that traditional notions of authorship — rooted in nineteenth-century romantic individualism — are simply ill-suited to a generative collaborator. So rather than asking whether AI art is "real", the more productive question is what authorship now means in a co-creative pipeline. The category itself, I'd argue, is overdue for revision.
Q2. Should museum entry be free?
PEEL answer
Point: I'd argue in favour of free entry as a default, though with important caveats around funding sustainability.

Evidence: The UK's 2001 free-admission policy, evaluated by Bertacchini and Pignataro in the Journal of Cultural Economics (2023), tripled annual visits at national museums and broadened socioeconomic representation, particularly among lower-income households. However, an OECD 2022 report on cultural funding warned that the Anglo-American model now depends precariously on private patronage and government subsidy.

Explanation: What this suggests is that free entry is genuinely democratising, but only sustainable when paired with robust public funding — otherwise it risks accelerating the commodification of museum spaces through gift shops and corporate sponsorship.
Link: Free entry, then, is a means rather than an end.

The UK's 2001 free-admission policy, evaluated by Bertacchini and Pignataro in the Journal of Cultural Economics in 2023, tripled annual visits and broadened socioeconomic representation. Yet the OECD's 2022 cultural funding report warned the Anglo-American model now depends precariously on private patronage. What this suggests is that free entry is genuinely democratising, but only sustainable when paired with robust public funding — otherwise it risks accelerating the commodification of museum spaces. Free entry, in short, is a means rather than an end.
Q3. Are NFTs fundamentally changing how we value art?
PEEL answer
Point: I'd say the NFT moment exposed something real about art markets, even as the bubble itself has largely deflated.

Evidence: Beeple's "Everydays" sold for USD 69.3 million at Christie's in March 2021; yet a 2024 Chainalysis report documented that NFT trading volumes collapsed by roughly 95% from their 2022 peak. A Journal of Cultural Economics paper by Whitaker (2023) argued that NFTs disrupted not so much aesthetic valuation as the legal architecture of provenance and royalties.

Explanation: What the episode revealed, on closer inspection, is that scarcity in the digital era is a legal-technical construct rather than a material one — which is genuinely consequential for artist remuneration.
Link: The hype was evanescent; the underlying provenance question, less so.

Beeple's Everydays sold for USD 69.3 million at Christie's in March 2021, but Chainalysis's 2024 report documented that NFT trading volumes collapsed by roughly 95% from their 2022 peak. What the episode revealed is that digital scarcity is a legal-technical construct, not a material one — and that has genuine implications for artist remuneration. The hype was evanescent; the provenance question, less so.

1. Section Type

blocks.text: 3. Predict 3 Ideas
The lecture will probably distinguish casual viewing from genuine aesthetic experience.
Patronage — historical and modern — will be linked to who decides what counts as art.
Connoisseurship may be defended as a learned skill, not snobbery.
4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Welcome, all. This morning we explore a question that has vexed cultural theorists since Kant: what exactly happens when we encounter a great work of art? We call this the aesthetic experience, and it is far stranger than mere enjoyment.

> Kant argued — and contemporary neuroaesthetics increasingly supports him — that genuine aesthetic encounter involves disinterested pleasure: a momentary suspension of utility, ego and even language. You don't ask what a Rothko is for; you simply stand before it and undergo something. Functional MRI studies at University College London show measurable activation of the default-mode network — the brain's introspective circuitry — within milliseconds of viewing a piece deemed beautiful by the subject.

> But aesthetic experiences don't happen in a vacuum. Someone, somewhere, has to fund the conditions for them. Enter cultural patronage — the system by which societies underwrite art. Historically this meant the Medici bankrolling Michelangelo; today it means state subsidies, corporate sponsorship, and private foundations. Critics object that public funding amounts to taxing nurses to subsidise the bourgeois leisure of opera-goers — and they're not wrong to raise the question. The strongest counter-argument is that without public patronage, the arts collapse into a market that rewards only the commercially palatable, and avant-garde experimentation dies first.

Now, before we examine those attendance figures, I want to interrogate the Kantian picture I sketched earlier, because, well, it has come in for some pointed criticism that I don't think we should sweep aside. The objection runs like this. Kant's "disinterested pleasure" assumes a universal, culture-neutral faculty of taste — as though a beholder from any society, stripped of context, would respond identically to the beautiful. The sociologist Pierre Bourdieu demolished that assumption rather thoroughly. In his study Distinction, he argued that aesthetic judgement is not innate at all; it is, um, a marker of class — an acquired disposition that the educated bourgeoisie mistake for a natural endowment. [pause] So what feels like spontaneous, disinterested rapture before a Rothko may in fact be the quiet operation of inherited cultural capital.

That reframing sharpens, rather than dissolves, the connoisseurship question I raised. If the period eye is genuinely teachable — and Baxandall thought it was — then the inequality Bourdieu diagnosed is contingent, not fixed. It follows from unequal access to training, not from any deficit of innate sensibility. Which is, I'd suggest, a rather hopeful corollary buried inside a pessimistic critique.

Let me also add an empirical complication to the neuroaesthetics story. Recent work distinguishes two quite different responses we lazily lump together as "beauty": the smooth, fluent pleasure of easily processed harmony, and the far stranger experience of the sublime — awe shading into something close to fear, the response a Caspar David Friedrich landscape or a vast cathedral can provoke. Imaging studies suggest these recruit partly divergent networks. [pause] So "aesthetic experience" may not be one phenomenon but a family of them. Now, all of this — the class-coding of taste, the teachability of the trained eye, the divided neurology of beauty — bears directly on how a society ought to fund and distribute access to art, and it's to that public-policy reckoning that I now want to turn…

> Finally, connoisseurship. This term has acquired a whiff of elitism, but properly understood, it simply names the trained capacity to perceive distinctions a novice cannot. A connoisseur isn't smarter — she has, through hundreds of hours of careful looking, developed what art historian Michael Baxandall called the period eye. That skill is teachable, and it is, I'd argue, a public good worth democratising. Now, turning to the data on museum attendance since 2010…

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~287 words)

The question of how the arts should be funded — through generous government subsidy or through private patronage — has long divided cultural policymakers. Although both models have something to offer, I believe public funding must remain the backbone of arts policy.

Supporters of heavy subsidy point out that the arts are repositories of national heritage and therefore a public good. What organisations such as the Arts Council in the United Kingdom tend to emphasise is accessibility: free or low-cost entry to museums, galleries and theatres ensures that cultural appreciation is not confined to the wealthy. Without public money, ticket prices would likely rise, and many regional institutions would face existential financial pressure, leaving the arts as a domain of elitism rather than shared inheritance.

Those who prefer private patronage, by contrast, argue that philanthropy research shows donors to be more flexible and responsive than ministries. Wealthy patrons and corporate sponsors can finance ambitious projects quickly, and market signals can help filter out work that fails to find an audience. Iconic cultural buildings, such as the Guggenheim Bilbao's mixed-funding model, have been built largely through private giving and have revitalised entire urban economies.

In my view, relying exclusively on either model would be unwise. Subsidy alone risks creating dependence on shifting political priorities, while private patronage alone tends to concentrate cultural power among a small donor class. A hybrid system, with state funding as the floor and philanthropy as a supplement, seems the most balanced approach.

To conclude, while both public subsidy and private patronage have legitimate roles, I lean toward continued government support as the central pillar. This is the only arrangement that genuinely safeguards both artistic accessibility and the cultural heritage that defines a nation.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~301 words)

Few questions in cultural policy are as contested as how the arts ought to be funded. While advocates of heavy state subsidy and proponents of private patronage each marshal substantial arguments, my position is that public funding must remain the structural backbone, complemented — not replaced — by philanthropy.

Those who defend generous subsidy argue, with considerable force, that the arts function as repositories of collective heritage and therefore meet the classical definition of a public good. What Arts Council research consistently demonstrates is that subsidised entry democratises access: were museums and regional theatres reliant solely on ticket revenue, they would almost certainly drift toward elitism, catering predominantly to affluent urban audiences. Public investment, in this view, is what prevents the arts from becoming the exclusive preserve of the well-off.

Equally serious, however, is the case for private patronage. Philanthropy research suggests that donors and corporate sponsors tend to provide flexible, fast-moving capital that ministries, constrained by electoral cycles, often cannot match. Landmark institutions — the Guggenheim Bilbao among them — illustrate how private giving, intelligently leveraged, can revitalise entire urban economies. So influential has private patronage become in the contemporary art market that several countries have re-engineered their tax codes to encourage cultural donations.

My own view is that the dichotomy is false. Exclusive reliance on subsidy risks subordinating culture to shifting political priorities; exclusive reliance on philanthropy risks concentrating curatorial power in a narrow donor class. A hybrid model — substantial public funding as the floor, philanthropic giving as accelerator — best preserves both accessibility and innovation.

To conclude, although heavy subsidy and private patronage each carry weight, I incline toward a mixed system anchored by public funding. Only such a settlement, in my considered view, can simultaneously safeguard cultural heritage, democratise access, and remain responsive to artistic experimentation.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc cao cấp xuyên suốt (inversion 'So influential has private patronage become', cleft 'What Arts Council research… demonstrates is', đảo ngữ điều kiện 'were museums… reliant solely') trong khi Band 7 chỉ dùng một cleft đơn.

•  Band 8 dẫn bằng chứng cụ thể và sắc bén hơn ('re-engineered their tax codes', 'constrained by electoral cycles') cùng nominalisation dày ('the dichotomy is false', 'exclusive reliance on subsidy'), nâng Task Response và Lexical Resource.
•  Band 8 dùng cohesion tinh tế với em-dash xen ('complemented — not replaced — by') và connector học thuật ('Equally serious, however', 'in my considered view'), register nhất quán hơn bản 7.

vocabulary.definition_vi: vô giá
vocabulary.example: The Mona Lisa is considered a priceless masterpiece; you simply cannot put a price tag on it.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'price' (giá) + '-less' (không có) → không thể định giá vì quá quý giá.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nhà bảo trợ — người giàu có hoặc có ảnh hưởng, hỗ trợ tài chính cho nghệ sĩ hoặc tổ chức nghệ thuật.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Wealthy **patrons** in Renaissance Florence funded some of the greatest artworks in history.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'pater' (cha, gốc Latin) → patron → người 'đỡ đầu' như một người cha cho nghệ sĩ.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'patron' (nhà bảo trợ) với 'patient' (bệnh nhân) — hoàn toàn khác nghĩa dù gần giống về hình thức.
vocabulary.definition_en: a wealthy or influential person who gives financial or other support to an artist, cause, or institution
vocabulary.definition_vi: nhà bảo trợ
vocabulary.example: Wealthy patrons in Renaissance Florence funded some of the greatest artworks in history.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'pater' (cha, gốc Latin) → patron → người 'đỡ đầu' như một người cha cho nghệ sĩ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đương đại — thuộc về hoặc xảy ra ở thời điểm hiện tại; mang phong cách hiện đại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The gallery is hosting an exhibition of **contemporary** sculpture next week.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'con-' (cùng) + 'tempus' (thời gian, gốc Latin) → cùng thời điểm hiện tại → đương đại.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Contemporary' có thể vừa là tính từ (đương đại) vừa là danh từ (người cùng thời); phân biệt theo ngữ cảnh.
vocabulary.definition_en: belonging to or occurring in the present time; modern in style or character
vocabulary.definition_vi: đương đại
vocabulary.example: The gallery is hosting an exhibition of contemporary sculpture next week.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'con-' (cùng) + 'tempus' (thời gian, gốc Latin) → cùng thời điểm hiện tại → đương đại.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Kho lưu trữ — nơi cất giữ các vật phẩm văn hoá hoặc tri thức quý giá.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The national museum serves as a **repository** for the country's most valuable cultural artefacts.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
're-' (lại) + 'ponere' (đặt, gốc Latin) → nơi đặt/cất giữ mọi thứ lại → kho lưu trữ.
vocabulary.common_error: Đi với giới từ 'for' hoặc 'of', không phải 'in'; số nhiều là 'repositories'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a place, building, or receptacle where things are or may be stored, especially cultural or historical objects
vocabulary.definition_vi: nơi lưu trữ, kho tàng (văn hoá, tri thức)
vocabulary.example: The national museum serves as a repository for the country's most valuable cultural artefacts.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 're-' (lại) + 'ponere' (đặt, gốc Latin) → nơi đặt/cất giữ mọi thứ lại → kho lưu trữ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Trợ cấp, hỗ trợ tài chính (thường từ ngân sách nhà nước) để giữ giá thấp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The government should **subsidise** the arts to keep ticket prices low for everyone.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'sub-' (bên dưới) + 'sidere' (ngồi, gốc Latin) → hỗ trợ 'ngồi bên dưới' nâng đỡ tài chính.
vocabulary.common_error: Chính tả Anh-Anh dùng '-ise' (subsidise), Anh-Mỹ dùng '-ize' (subsidize); danh từ là 'subsidy', không phải 'subsidisation' trong văn nói.
vocabulary.definition_en: to support an organisation or activity financially, especially with public funds, to keep prices low
vocabulary.definition_vi: trợ cấp, tài trợ (bằng ngân sách công)
vocabulary.example: The government should subsidise the arts to keep ticket prices low for everyone.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'sub-' (bên dưới) + 'sidere' (ngồi, gốc Latin) → hỗ trợ 'ngồi bên dưới' nâng đỡ tài chính.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự bảo trợ, đặc biệt là hỗ trợ tài chính dành cho nghệ sĩ hoặc tổ chức văn hoá.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> State **patronage** of the arts has allowed many struggling theatres to survive difficult economic periods.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'patron' (nhà bảo trợ) + -age (trạng thái) → patronage → hành động/mối quan hệ bảo trợ.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'patronage' (sự bảo trợ) với 'patronising' (kẻ cả, coi thường) — cùng gốc nhưng nghĩa phái sinh khác hẳn.
vocabulary.definition_en: the support, especially financial, given by a patron to an artist, institution, or cause
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự bảo trợ
vocabulary.example: State patronage of the arts has allowed many struggling theatres to survive difficult economic periods.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'patron' (nhà bảo trợ) + -age (trạng thái) → patronage → hành động/mối quan hệ bảo trợ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tiên phong — mang tính thử nghiệm mới mẻ, thách thức các chuẩn mực nghệ thuật thông thường.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Critics were divided over the **avant-garde** installation, calling it either groundbreaking or needlessly obscure.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Tiếng Pháp 'avant' (phía trước) + 'garde' (đội canh gác) → đội tiên phong đi trước thời đại.
vocabulary.common_error: Từ mượn tiếng Pháp, giữ nguyên dấu gạch nối 'avant-garde'; phát âm không có 't' rõ ở cuối 'avant'.
vocabulary.definition_en: new and experimental ideas or methods in art, especially those that challenge conventional norms
vocabulary.definition_vi: tiên phong, tiền vệ (nghệ thuật thử nghiệm)
vocabulary.example: Critics were divided over the avant-garde installation, calling it either groundbreaking or needlessly obscure.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Tiếng Pháp 'avant' (phía trước) + 'garde' (đội canh gác) → đội tiên phong đi trước thời đại.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Gợi cảm xúc — có khả năng khơi dậy hình ảnh, ký ức hoặc cảm xúc mạnh mẽ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Van Gogh's **evocative** brushstrokes seem to capture the raw emotion of the landscape itself.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'evoke' (gợi lên) + -ative → evocative → có khả năng gợi lên cảm xúc, hình ảnh.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'evocative' (gợi cảm xúc) với 'provocative' (khiêu khích) — hai từ khác nghĩa dù âm gần giống.
vocabulary.definition_en: bringing strong images, memories, or feelings to mind
vocabulary.definition_vi: gợi cảm xúc, gợi hình ảnh mạnh mẽ
vocabulary.example: Van Gogh's evocative brushstrokes seem to capture the raw emotion of the landscape itself.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'evoke' (gợi lên) + -ative → evocative → có khả năng gợi lên cảm xúc, hình ảnh.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vốn văn hoá — tài sản phi tài chính như học vấn, gu thẩm mỹ, hiểu biết nghệ thuật giúp nâng cao vị thế xã hội.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Attending the opera regularly can help a person accumulate significant **cultural capital** in certain social circles.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'cultural' (văn hoá) + 'capital' (vốn) → tri thức, gu thẩm mỹ hoạt động như một loại vốn xã hội.
vocabulary.common_error: Thuật ngữ xã hội học của Bourdieu; không đếm được, không có số nhiều 'cultural capitals'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the non-financial social assets, such as education, taste, and knowledge of the arts, that promote social status
vocabulary.definition_vi: vốn văn hoá
vocabulary.example: Attending the opera regularly can help a person accumulate significant cultural capital in certain social circles.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'cultural' (văn hoá) + 'capital' (vốn) → tri thức, gu thẩm mỹ hoạt động như một loại vốn xã hội.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Người sành sỏi, có kiến thức chuyên sâu và gu thẩm mỹ tinh tế, đặc biệt trong nghệ thuật.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Only a true **connoisseur** would notice the subtle brushwork techniques hidden in the background of the painting.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Tiếng Pháp 'connaître' (biết, hiểu rõ) → connoisseur → người hiểu biết sâu sắc, sành sỏi.
vocabulary.common_error: Từ mượn tiếng Pháp, phát âm phần cuối là /-sɜː/, không đọc 's' như âm 'z'; không phát âm chữ 's' đôi.
vocabulary.definition_en: a person with expert knowledge and refined judgement, especially in the fine arts or matters of taste
vocabulary.definition_vi: người sành sỏi, người am hiểu tinh tường
vocabulary.example: Only a true connoisseur would notice the subtle brushwork techniques hidden in the background of the painting.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Tiếng Pháp 'connaître' (biết, hiểu rõ) → connoisseur → người hiểu biết sâu sắc, sành sỏi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Di sản — truyền thống, thành tựu và các giá trị văn hoá được kế thừa từ các thế hệ trước.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Traditional water-puppet theatre is a vital part of the country's artistic **heritage**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'heir' (người thừa kế) → heritage → những gì được truyền lại cho thế hệ sau.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'heritage' (di sản, danh từ trừu tượng không đếm được) với 'heirloom' (vật gia truyền cụ thể).
vocabulary.definition_en: the traditions, achievements, and cultural artefacts inherited from previous generations
vocabulary.definition_vi: di sản (văn hoá, nghệ thuật)
vocabulary.example: Traditional water-puppet theatre is a vital part of the country's artistic heritage.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'heir' (người thừa kế) → heritage → những gì được truyền lại cho thế hệ sau.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khoa học thần kinh thẩm mỹ — nghiên cứu cơ chế não bộ đằng sau trải nghiệm thẩm mỹ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Neuroaesthetics** researchers use fMRI scans to investigate why certain paintings trigger a strong emotional response.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'neuro-' (thần kinh) + 'aesthetics' (mỹ học) → nghiên cứu não bộ phản ứng thế nào với cái đẹp.
vocabulary.common_error: Thuật ngữ liên ngành mới (khoa học thần kinh + mỹ học); chia động từ số ít như một ngành học duy nhất.
vocabulary.definition_en: the scientific study of the neural (brain) basis of aesthetic experiences, such as appreciating art or beauty
vocabulary.definition_vi: khoa học thần kinh thẩm mỹ
vocabulary.example: Neuroaesthetics researchers use fMRI scans to investigate why certain paintings trigger a strong emotional response.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'neuro-' (thần kinh) + 'aesthetics' (mỹ học) → nghiên cứu não bộ phản ứng thế nào với cái đẹp.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khoái cảm vô tư — sự thưởng thức thuần tuý vì bản thân cái đẹp, không vì mục đích cá nhân hay thực dụng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Kant argued that a true aesthetic experience arises from **disinterested pleasure**, judging beauty without regard to personal desire or usefulness.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'dis-' (không) + 'interested' (có lợi ích cá nhân) → thưởng thức mà không vụ lợi, thuần khiết.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'disinterested' (vô tư, khách quan) với 'uninterested' (không quan tâm) — hai từ khác nghĩa hoàn toàn dù dễ lẫn.
vocabulary.definition_en: (in Kantian aesthetics) enjoyment of something purely for its own sake, without personal or practical interest
vocabulary.definition_vi: khoái cảm vô tư (thẩm mỹ thuần tuý, không vụ lợi)
vocabulary.example: Kant argued that a true aesthetic experience arises from disinterested pleasure, judging beauty without regard to personal desire or usefulness.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'dis-' (không) + 'interested' (có lợi ích cá nhân) → thưởng thức mà không vụ lợi, thuần khiết.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Ngôn ngữ chung — hình thức biểu đạt được cho là ai cũng có thể hiểu, không phân biệt tiếng mẹ đẻ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Music is often described as a **universal language** that connects people across borders.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'universal' (phổ quát) + 'language' (ngôn ngữ) → thứ mà ai cũng hiểu, không cần lời.
collocations: art transcends as a universal language
vocabulary.common_error: Thường dùng ẩn dụ (music/art), không phải nghĩa đen về một ngôn ngữ thật sự được cả thế giới nói.
vocabulary.definition_en: a form of communication or expression believed to be understood by people everywhere, regardless of native tongue
vocabulary.definition_vi: ngôn ngữ chung của nhân loại
vocabulary.example: Music is often described as a universal language that connects people across borders.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'universal' (phổ quát) + 'language' (ngôn ngữ) → thứ mà ai cũng hiểu, không cần lời.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Ca từ, lời của một bài hát.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The melody is catchy, but the **lyrics** of the song are deeply moving and poetic.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc từ 'lyre' (đàn lia cổ Hy Lạp) → lyrics → lời hát đi kèm với nhạc cụ.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn ở dạng số nhiều 'lyrics' khi nói về lời một bài hát; 'a lyric' số ít mang nghĩa khác (một thể thơ trữ tình).
vocabulary.definition_en: the words of a song
vocabulary.definition_vi: lời bài hát, ca từ
vocabulary.example: The melody is catchy, but the lyrics of the song are deeply moving and poetic.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc từ 'lyre' (đàn lia cổ Hy Lạp) → lyrics → lời hát đi kèm với nhạc cụ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tác phẩm sắp đặt — nghệ thuật được bố trí trong một không gian cụ thể, thường quy mô lớn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The modern artist is famous for creating massive 3D video **installations** in public spaces.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'install' (lắp đặt) + -ation → tác phẩm được 'lắp đặt' choán trọn một không gian trưng bày.
vocabulary.common_error: Trong nghệ thuật, 'installation' chỉ tác phẩm sắp đặt không gian, khác với nghĩa thông thường 'lắp đặt thiết bị'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a piece of art constructed or arranged, often on a large scale, within a specific space or environment
vocabulary.definition_vi: tác phẩm sắp đặt
vocabulary.example: The modern artist is famous for creating massive 3D video installations in public spaces.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'install' (lắp đặt) + -ation → tác phẩm được 'lắp đặt' choán trọn một không gian trưng bày.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Buổi ra mắt — lần đầu tiên xuất hiện hoặc biểu diễn trước công chúng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The young singer made her professional **debut** at the Royal Opera House last night.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Tiếng Pháp 'début' (khởi đầu) → debut → lần xuất hiện đầu tiên trước công chúng.
vocabulary.common_error: Từ mượn tiếng Pháp, chữ 't' cuối không phát âm; thường đi với động từ 'make' chứ không phải 'do'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a person's first public appearance or performance in a particular role or activity
vocabulary.definition_vi: buổi ra mắt, màn trình diễn đầu tiên
vocabulary.example: The young singer made her professional debut at the Royal Opera House last night.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Tiếng Pháp 'début' (khởi đầu) → debut → lần xuất hiện đầu tiên trước công chúng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nghệ sĩ đường phố — người biểu diễn âm nhạc hoặc nghệ thuật nơi công cộng để nhận tiền thưởng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We stopped in the subway to watch a talented **busker** playing the saxophone.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'busk' nghe gần 'bus stop' → nghệ sĩ chơi nhạc ở nơi công cộng như bến xe, phố đi bộ.
vocabulary.common_error: Danh từ chỉ người, động từ tương ứng là 'busk' (không phải 'busker' dùng như động từ).
vocabulary.definition_en: a person who performs music or other entertainment in public places for donations
vocabulary.definition_vi: nghệ sĩ đường phố
vocabulary.example: We stopped in the subway to watch a talented busker playing the saxophone.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'busk' nghe gần 'bus stop' → nghệ sĩ chơi nhạc ở nơi công cộng như bến xe, phố đi bộ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Dân chủ hoá khả năng tiếp cận — mở rộng cơ hội thụ hưởng văn hoá, nghệ thuật cho đông đảo công chúng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Free museum entry is a powerful way of **democratising access** to culture for lower-income families.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'democracy' (dân chủ) → democratise → mở rộng quyền tiếp cận cho tất cả mọi người, không chỉ tầng lớp ưu tú.
vocabulary.common_error: Chính tả Anh-Anh dùng '-ise' (democratising), không phải '-izing' kiểu Mỹ.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of making something, such as art or culture, available to a much wider range of people
vocabulary.definition_vi: dân chủ hoá khả năng tiếp cận
vocabulary.example: Free museum entry is a powerful way of democratising access to culture for lower-income families.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'democracy' (dân chủ) → democratise → mở rộng quyền tiếp cận cho tất cả mọi người, không chỉ tầng lớp ưu tú.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Những nhà bảo trợ siêu giàu — cá nhân có tài sản ròng cực lớn hỗ trợ tài chính cho các tổ chức văn hoá.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Many major galleries now rely heavily on **high-net-worth patrons** rather than public funding to stay afloat.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'high net worth' (tài sản ròng cao, thuật ngữ tài chính) + 'patrons' (nhà bảo trợ) → người siêu giàu tài trợ nghệ thuật.
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm danh từ ghép có gạch nối khi đứng trước danh từ: 'high-net-worth patrons', không tách rời.
vocabulary.definition_en: extremely wealthy individuals who provide significant financial support to institutions such as museums or theatres
vocabulary.definition_vi: những nhà bảo trợ có giá trị tài sản ròng cao
vocabulary.example: Many major galleries now rely heavily on high-net-worth patrons rather than public funding to stay afloat.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'high net worth' (tài sản ròng cao, thuật ngữ tài chính) + 'patrons' (nhà bảo trợ) → người siêu giàu tài trợ nghệ thuật.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mã token không thể thay thế — chứng nhận sở hữu số hoá độc nhất được ghi trên blockchain, thường dùng cho tác phẩm nghệ thuật số.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The **NFT** moment exposed something real about digital ownership, even as the speculative bubble eventually deflated.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'non-' (không) + 'fungible' (có thể thay thế) + 'token' (mã) → mã số độc nhất, không thể đổi lấy cái khác giống hệt.
vocabulary.common_error: Thường viết tắt 'NFT'; 'fungible' nghĩa là 'có thể thay thế được', nên 'non-fungible' = không thể thay thế, mỗi token là duy nhất.
vocabulary.definition_en: a unique digital certificate, recorded on a blockchain, used to represent ownership of a digital artwork or asset
vocabulary.definition_vi: mã token không thể thay thế (chứng nhận sở hữu tác phẩm số)
vocabulary.example: The NFT moment exposed something real about digital ownership, even as the speculative bubble eventually deflated.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'non-' (không) + 'fungible' (có thể thay thế) + 'token' (mã) → mã số độc nhất, không thể đổi lấy cái khác giống hệt.
